# The data

The examples use `splat.sim`, the bifurcating trajectory of the
[Quick start](https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/scMaSigPro.html)
vignette: 200 cells on two paths, `Path1` and `Path2`, with the simulated
step of each cell as its pseudotime. splatter [@zappia2017] stores how it
simulated each gene; a gene whose differential expression factor
(`DEFacPath1`, `DEFacPath2`) is not 1 on a path changes along that path.

```{r load-data, message = FALSE}
library(scMaSigPro)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(ggplot2)

data("splat.sim", package = "scMaSigPro")
truth <- rowData(splat.sim)
changes <- truth$DEFacPath1 != 1 | truth$DEFacPath2 != 1
names(changes) <- rownames(truth)
sum(changes)

scmp_ob <- as_scmp(splat.sim,
    verbose = FALSE,
    additional_params = list(
        labels_exist = TRUE,
        exist_ptime_col = "Step",
        exist_path_col = "Group"
    )
)
```

# Bins

A single cell holds few reads of each gene, and many of its counts are
zero. scMaSigPro therefore pools the cells of each path into bins along
pseudotime and adds up their counts into a pseudo-bulk count per bin, which
raises the signal-to-noise ratio; the bins, numbered in order along
pseudotime, become the time points of a time course, as in maSigPro
[@srivastava2024, sec. 2.1].

`sc.squeeze()` divides the pseudotime range of each path into bins of equal
width. Each bin is closed on the left and open on the right, except the last
bin of a path, which is closed on both ends, so a cell on the border of two
bins goes to the later one. The number of bins comes from a histogram rule
(`bin_method`), applied to the n cells of the path:

* `"Sturges"` (the default): log~2~(n) + 1 bins [@sturges1926];
* `"Sqrt"`: the square root of n;
* `"Rice"`: 2 n^1/3^;
* `"Doane"`: Sturges' rule plus a term for the skewness of the pseudotime
    [@doane1976];
* `"Freedman.Diaconis"` and `"Scott.Normal"`: bins of width
    2 IQR / n^1/3^ and 3.49 sd / n^1/3^ [@freedman1981; @scott1979], turned
    into a number of bins by dividing the range of the pseudotime by the
    width.

The number of bins is then multiplied by the drop factor `drop_fac` (at
least 0.3; below 1 for fewer, wider bins) and rounded up. For data with
many zeros, the article recommends a lower drop factor, which gives fewer
bins with more cells each; it also suggests the rule of Rice for
pseudotime values that span a broad range and that of Doane for skewed
ones [@srivastava2024, sec. 4]. The number of bins of each rule for the two
paths of `splat.sim`:

```{r bin-rules}
rules <- c(
    "Sturges", "Sqrt", "Rice", "Doane", "Freedman.Diaconis", "Scott.Normal"
)
sapply(rules, function(rule) {
    table(cDense(sc.squeeze(scmp_ob, bin_method = rule))$Path)
})
```

Bins of equal width hold different numbers of cells where cells are dense or
sparse along the pseudotime. `split_bins = TRUE` divides the bins of a path
that hold more cells than the mean plus the standard deviation of its bin
sizes, and `prune_bins = TRUE` removes those that hold fewer than the mean
minus the standard deviation [@srivastava2024, sec. 2.2]. `fill_gaps`
renumbers the bins after pruning, and `drop_trails` cuts the longer paths
to the binned pseudotime of the shortest.

```{r bin-split, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Tile plot of the bins of splat.sim after splitting the bins that hold the
#|   most cells.
split_ob <- sc.squeeze(scmp_ob, split_bins = TRUE)
table(cDense(split_ob)$Path)
plotBinTile(split_ob)
```

Fewer, larger bins give each pseudo-bulk count more cells and the model
fewer points; more, smaller bins the reverse. A polynomial of
degree d has d + 1 coefficients per path, so each path needs more than d + 1
bins to leave residual degrees of freedom for the test.

# The model

## A polynomial in pseudotime per path

`sc.set.poly()` builds the design of the model of maSigPro
[@conesa2006; @nueda2014]. With two paths and a polynomial of degree 2, the
expected count $\mu$ of a gene in a bin at binned pseudotime $t$ is modelled
as

$$
\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 t^2
    + \beta_3 z + \beta_4 t z + \beta_5 t^2 z + \text{offset},
$$

where $z$ is a dummy variable, 1 for the bins of the second path and 0 for
those of the reference path [@srivastava2024, sec. 2.3]. $\beta_0$,
$\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ describe the profile of the reference path;
$\beta_3$, $\beta_4$ and $\beta_5$ are the differences of the second path
from it, in level, slope and curvature. With more paths, every path but the
reference gets a dummy and its products with the powers of $t$.

```{r design}
scmp_ob <- sc.squeeze(scmp_ob)
scmp_ob <- sc.set.poly(scmp_ob, poly_degree = 2)
showPoly(scmp_ob)
head(predictors(scmp_ob), 3)
head(pathAssign(scmp_ob), 3)
```

`predictors()` returns the design, one row per bin and one column per term
besides the intercept, and `pathAssign()` the binned pseudotime and the path
of each bin, the `edesign` of maSigPro.

## The reference path

The reference path is the path the others are compared with. Without
`reference`, `sc.set.poly()` takes the first path of the bins: the first
level of the path column when it is a factor, and otherwise the first label
in C-locale (byte) order, in every locale. The full model is the same with
any reference, written in other terms, so the test of each gene does not
change; the coefficients, the terms that `sc.t.fit()` selects and the
`"groups"` lists of `sc.filter()` describe the chosen comparison.

```{r reference}
ref1 <- sc.p.vector(sc.set.poly(scmp_ob, poly_degree = 1), verbose = FALSE)
ref2 <- sc.p.vector(
    sc.set.poly(scmp_ob, poly_degree = 1, reference = "Path2"),
    verbose = FALSE
)
showPoly(ref2)
all.equal(scmpResults(ref1)$p_value, scmpResults(ref2)$p_value)
identical(scmpResults(ref1)$non_flat, scmpResults(ref2)$non_flat)
```

The [Shared root](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/shared-root.html)
vignette chooses the reference in a trajectory with more paths.

## The negative binomial distribution and theta

The counts of a gene vary more between bins than a Poisson distribution
allows, so the default model is negative binomial [@srivastava2024, sec.
2.3]. Its family is `MASS::negative.binomial(theta = 10)` [@venables2002],
whose variance is $\mu + \mu^2 / \theta$: `theta` is fixed at 10 by
default, as in maSigPro, and any other theta or family can be passed to
`family`.

`theta_estimate` estimates theta from the data instead: `"gene"` estimates
it by maximum likelihood on the full model of each gene and fits the gene
with its own theta, and `"global"` fits every gene with the median of these
estimates. `sc.t.fit()` and `plotDiagnostics()` use the same theta.

```{r theta}
theta_ob <- sc.p.vector(scmp_ob, theta_estimate = "gene", verbose = FALSE)
showParams(theta_ob)[showParams(theta_ob)$parameters == "distribution", ]
```

## The offset

Bins hold different numbers of cells, so their pseudo-bulk counts differ in
total even for a gene that does not change. The offset corrects for this:
it is the logarithm of a size factor per bin, added to the linear predictor
with a fixed coefficient of 1 [@srivastava2024, sec. 2.3]. The size factors
are those of the median-of-ratios method [@anders2010; @love2014]: the size
factor of a bin is the median, over the genes, of the ratio of the gene's
count in the bin to its geometric mean over all bins. The worked example of
the article's supplementary section S1.3, three genes in three bins:

```{r offset-example}
counts <- rbind(
    Gene1 = c(Bin1 = 100, Bin2 = 150, Bin3 = 200),
    Gene2 = c(Bin1 = 200, Bin2 = 300, Bin3 = 250),
    Gene3 = c(Bin1 = 300, Bin2 = 450, Bin3 = 500)
)
log_geo_mean <- rowMeans(log(counts))
size_factor <- exp(apply(log(counts) - log_geo_mean, 2, median))
size_factor
log(size_factor)
```

`sc.p.vector()` computes them in the same way from the pseudo-bulk counts
of every gene without a zero count, and `sc.t.fit()` uses the same offsets.
On `splat.sim` the size factors follow the number of cells of the bins:

```{r offset-bins, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Size factor of each bin against its number of cells: the size factor grows
#|   with the number of cells.
bulk <- eDense(scmp_ob)
log_geo_mean <- rowMeans(log(bulk))
use <- is.finite(log_geo_mean)
bins <- cDense(scmp_ob)
bins$size_factor <- exp(
    apply(log(bulk[use, rownames(bins)]) - log_geo_mean[use], 2, median)
)
ggplot(bins, aes(scmp_bin_size, size_factor, colour = Path)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "Cells in the bin", y = "Size factor") +
    theme_minimal()
```

Without the offset (`offset = FALSE`), this difference between bins stays
in the counts of every gene, and on `splat.sim` far fewer genes pass the
test, as the table at the end shows.

## The link

The link function relates the expected count to the polynomial. The
default, the log link, makes the terms multiplicative and is the one the
offset needs. `link = "identity"` fits the expected count itself; it needs
`offset = FALSE`, and with a negative binomial family the fitted mean of a
gene can become negative, which `glm()` refuses or warns about. For data
that are not counts, such as log-normalised values, `family = gaussian()`
with `offset = FALSE` fits the linear model of maSigPro for microarrays, as
the [maSigPro and the ScMaSigPro class](
    https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/masigpro-and-class.html)
vignette shows.

# The steps and their settings

## Testing each gene

`sc.p.vector()` fits the full model of each gene and tests it against the
model with the intercept only, which is a flat profile; the genes whose
adjusted p-value is at most `p_value` have a non-flat profile
[@srivastava2024, sec. 2.4]. The p-values are adjusted for the number of
genes with `mt_correction`, by default the method of Benjamini and Hochberg
[@benjamini1995], so `p_value` is a false discovery rate.

The default test, `test = "chisq"`, divides the difference in deviance by
the estimated dispersion and compares it with the chi-squared distribution,
as maSigPro does. With few bins, the estimate of the dispersion varies from
gene to gene and the test calls more genes significant than its level.
`test = "F"` accounts for that estimate and is more conservative:

```{r test}
chisq_ob <- sc.p.vector(scmp_ob, verbose = FALSE)
f_ob <- sc.p.vector(scmp_ob, test = "F", verbose = FALSE)
c(
    chisq = sum(scmpResults(chisq_ob)$non_flat),
    F = sum(scmpResults(f_ob)$non_flat)
)
```

Two filters leave genes with little expression out of the fit and out of
the correction: `min_counts`, the smallest total count of a gene over the
bins, and `min_bins_expressed`, the smallest number of bins in which its
count is above 0. Both are 0 by default.

## Selecting the terms

`sc.t.fit()` selects, for each gene with a non-flat profile, the terms of
its model that are significant at `p_value`: backward selection by default,
which starts from the full model and removes the least significant term
while its p-value is above the level, and forward or two-way selection with
`selection_method` [@conesa2006]. `nvar_correction = TRUE` divides the level
by the number of terms. The selected model of each gene, its p-value and
R-squared are in `showSol()`; its coefficients, with 0 for the terms not
selected, in `showCoeff()`; and the coefficients of each path's polynomial
in `showGroupCoeff()`.

```{r t-fit}
scmp_ob <- sc.t.fit(chisq_ob, verbose = FALSE)
head(showCoeff(scmp_ob), 3)
head(showGroupCoeff(scmp_ob), 3)
```

## Gene lists

`sc.filter()` keeps the genes whose selected model has an R-squared of at
least `rsq` and a p-value of at most `p_value`, and makes lists with `vars`:
`"all"`, one list; `"each"`, one list per term, with the genes whose term
has a p-value of at most `term_p_value`; `"groups"`, one list per path. With
`"groups"`, `intercept` says whether the dummies of the paths (`"dummy"`, the
default), these and the intercept (`"all"`), or neither (`"none"`) count.
`includeInflu = FALSE` leaves out the genes with influential observations.

For a generalised linear model, R-squared is the proportion of the deviance
of a gene that its model explains [@nueda2014; @srivastava2024, sec. 2.4],
so a higher `rsq` keeps fewer genes with clearer profiles:

```{r rsq}
vapply(c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9), function(r) {
    sum(scmpResults(sc.filter(scmp_ob, rsq = r, vars = "all"))$sig_all)
}, numeric(1))
each_ob <- sc.filter(scmp_ob, rsq = 0.7, vars = "each")
each_res <- scmpResults(each_ob)
colSums(as.data.frame(each_res[, grep("^sig_", colnames(each_res))]))
```

## Influential observations

A bin can pull the fit of a gene on its own. `sc.t.fit()` marks the genes
with a bin whose DFFITS and Cook's distance are both above the cut-off values of
`stats::influence.measures()`; `showInflu()` lists them. `plotDiagnostics()`
draws the residuals and the fit of the model of a gene of the lists of
`sc.filter()`, to judge whether to keep it:

```{r influence, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Four diagnostic plots of the model of one gene: normal Q-Q plot, residuals
#|   against fitted values, scale-location, and observed against predicted
#|   counts.
influential <- colnames(showInflu(scmp_ob))
influential
scmp_ob <- sc.filter(scmp_ob, rsq = 0.7, vars = "all")
listed <- rownames(scmpResults(scmp_ob))[scmpResults(scmp_ob)$sig_all]
plotDiagnostics(scmp_ob, intersect(influential, listed)[1])
```

## Reading the coefficients

`queryCoeff()` returns the coefficients of a group of terms, for the genes
whose selected model keeps every term of the group. With
`change = "increasing"` it keeps the genes whose coefficients of the group
add up to a positive number, or, with `strictly = TRUE`, are all positive;
`"decreasing"` does the same for negative numbers. Here the group is the
terms in pseudotime of the reference path, `Path1`:

```{r query}
rising <- queryCoeff(scmp_ob,
    query = "pseudotime", change = "increasing", verbose = FALSE
)
head(rising)
```

## Parallel fits

The fits of `sc.p.vector()` and `sc.t.fit()` run gene by gene through
BiocParallel [@biocparallel]. The default, `SerialParam()`, fits one gene
after another; `BPPARAM = BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(4)` (Linux and
macOS) or `BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SnowParam(4)` (any system) fits four at a
time. The results do not depend on the backend.

# The settings against the truth

The function below runs the workflow with some settings changed and counts
how many of the genes it finds were simulated to change (precision) and how
many of those it finds (recall), for the non-flat genes of `sc.p.vector()`
and for the list of `sc.filter(rsq = 0.7, vars = "all")`. Every run starts
from the settings of the
[Quick start](https://spriyansh.github.io/scMaSigPro/articles/scMaSigPro.html)
vignette: Sturges' rule, degree 1, the chi-squared test and theta 10.

```{r grid-function}
base_ob <- as_scmp(splat.sim,
    verbose = FALSE,
    additional_params = list(
        labels_exist = TRUE,
        exist_ptime_col = "Step",
        exist_path_col = "Group"
    )
)

score <- function(found) {
    tp <- sum(found & changes[names(found)])
    c(
        genes = sum(found), precision = tp / sum(found),
        recall = tp / sum(changes)
    )
}

run <- function(squeeze = list(), degree = 1, fit = list()) {
    ob <- do.call(sc.squeeze, c(list(base_ob), squeeze))
    ob <- sc.set.poly(ob, poly_degree = degree)
    ob <- do.call(sc.p.vector, c(list(ob, verbose = FALSE), fit))
    non_flat <- setNames(scmpResults(ob)$non_flat, rownames(scmpResults(ob)))
    ob <- sc.t.fit(ob, verbose = FALSE)
    ob <- sc.filter(ob, rsq = 0.7, vars = "all")
    listed <- setNames(scmpResults(ob)$sig_all, rownames(scmpResults(ob)))
    round(c(bins = nrow(cDense(ob)), score(non_flat), score(listed)), 2)
}
```

```{r grid}
grid <- rbind(
    "default" = run(),
    "bin_method = Sqrt" = run(squeeze = list(bin_method = "Sqrt")),
    "bin_method = Freedman.Diaconis" =
        run(squeeze = list(bin_method = "Freedman.Diaconis")),
    "drop_fac = 0.5" = run(squeeze = list(drop_fac = 0.5)),
    "split_bins = TRUE" = run(squeeze = list(split_bins = TRUE)),
    "prune_bins = TRUE" = run(squeeze = list(prune_bins = TRUE)),
    "poly_degree = 2" = run(degree = 2),
    "poly_degree = 3" = run(degree = 3),
    "test = F" = run(fit = list(test = "F")),
    "theta_estimate = gene" = run(fit = list(theta_estimate = "gene")),
    "offset = FALSE" = run(fit = list(offset = FALSE))
)
colnames(grid) <- c(
    "bins", "non-flat", "precision", "recall",
    "listed", "precision", "recall"
)
knitr::kable(grid)
```

```{r grid-numbers, include = FALSE}
with_offset <- grid[rownames(grid) != "offset = FALSE", ]
best_recall <- rownames(with_offset)[which.max(with_offset[, 4])]
best_precision <- rownames(with_offset)[which.max(with_offset[, 3])]
```

On this data set the offset matters most: without it, only
`r grid["offset = FALSE", 2]` genes pass the test. Among the other
settings, the highest recall of the non-flat genes is that of
`r best_recall` and the highest precision that of `r best_precision`; the F
test finds `r grid["test = F", 2]` non-flat genes instead of
`r grid["default", 2]`, with a precision of `r grid["test = F", 3]` and a
recall of `r grid["test = F", 4]`. Other data sets, with other numbers of
cells, depths and shapes of change, can favour other settings; a
simulation that resembles the data, as splatter makes them, is a way to
compare settings for a study.
